style: Textbook-quality scientific schematic for a computational electromagnetics user manual. Flat vector style on a white background, high contrast, thin dark outlines, generous whitespace, sans-serif labels. Colour code used in every figure: primary grid G and its quantities in blue, dual grid G-tilde and its quantities in orange, exact/topological items in dark grey, approximate/material items in green, failure or warning items in red. Colourblind-safe. Every label must be spelled exactly as listed in this brief; mathematical symbols must be typeset correctly (hats, tildes, subscripts, transposes). Do not add any number, value, equation, software name, product name, logo, watermark or title that is not listed in this brief. Prefer fewer, larger labels over many small ones. No 3D photorealism, no cartoon characters, no hand-drawn or xkcd style.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1: FIT stores integrals, not point values. Left: one primary cell of the grid G (blue cube) interlocked with the dual grid G-tilde (orange), whose vertex sits at the primary cell centre. A primary edge L_k carrying the voltage ê_k pierces its paired dual face Ã_k carrying the flux d̂_k; a primary face A_m carrying the flux b̂_m is pierced by its paired dual edge L̃_m carrying the voltage ĥ_m. Right: Faraday's law on one primary face is an exact sum of its four edge voltages with signs ±1 set by orientation.
figures.visual_intent: Two panels side by side. LEFT PANEL (about 60% width): an isometric wireframe of ONE primary cube cell drawn in blue. Highlight one blue edge, labelled 'L_k' and 'ê_k' with a small arrow along the edge. Through the middle of that edge draw a small orange square (the dual face) perpendicular to the edge, labelled 'Ã_k' and 'd̂_k', with the blue edge visibly passing through it. Shade one blue face of the cube lightly, labelled 'A_m' and 'b̂_m', and draw an orange line segment (dual edge) passing perpendicularly through the centre of that face, labelled 'L̃_m' and 'ĥ_m'. Mark the cube centre with an orange dot labelled 'ṽ_p'. Small legend: blue line 'primary grid G', orange line 'dual grid G̃'. RIGHT PANEL (about 40% width): a flat square face (blue) seen head-on, each edge drawn with its own orientation arrow along the coordinate axes: bottom edge arrow pointing right labelled 'ê_1', right edge arrow pointing up labelled 'ê_2', top edge arrow pointing right labelled 'ê_3', left edge arrow pointing up labelled 'ê_4'. Inside the face a thin curved counter-clockwise circulation arrow and a circled-dot symbol (normal out of the page) labelled 'b̂_m'. Small sign tags next to the edges: '+1' at the bottom and right edges (orientation agrees with the circulation), '−1' at the top and left edges (orientation opposes it). Under the face the single equation: 'ê_1 + ê_2 − ê_3 − ê_4 = −d b̂_m / dt' and below that, in grey, the words 'exact: no approximation'.

figures.caption: Figure 4.2: The Maxwell Grid Equations as a two-column diagram. The left column (primary grid G) and right column (dual grid G̃) are linked by integer incidence matrices C, S and C̃ = Cᵀ, S̃; the horizontal links are the material matrices M_ε and M_ν. Inset: the boundary of a boundary is empty, so every edge of a closed cube is traversed twice with opposite signs, giving S C = 0 and exact conservation of magnetic flux and charge.
figures.visual_intent: Main diagram (left 65%): a 'Tonti diagram' with two vertical columns of rounded boxes. LEFT column in blue, top to bottom: box 'ê (edge voltages)', down-arrow labelled 'C', box 'b̂ (face fluxes)', down-arrow labelled 'S', box '0'. RIGHT column in orange, top to bottom: box 'ĥ (dual edge voltages)', down-arrow labelled 'C̃ = Cᵀ', box 'd̂, ĵ (dual face fluxes)', down-arrow labelled 'S̃', box 'q (charge)'. The vertical arrows are dark grey and tagged with a small badge 'entries in {−1, 0, +1}: exact'. Two horizontal green double-headed arrows connect the columns: between 'ê' and 'd̂, ĵ' labelled 'M_ε' and between 'b̂' and 'ĥ' labelled 'M_ν', with a green badge 'material matrices: approximation'. Below the columns, four short equations in one row: 'C ê = −d b̂/dt', 'C̃ ĥ = d d̂/dt + ĵ', 'S b̂ = 0', 'S̃ d̂ = q'. INSET (right 35%): an exploded cube showing its six faces slightly separated, each face with a circulation arrow; one shared edge between two faces highlighted, showing two opposite arrows on it with tags '+1' and '−1' that cancel. Under the inset: '∂∂ = 0  ⇒  S C = 0' and 'magnetic flux and charge conserved to round-off'.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3: All spatial approximation in FIT lives in the material (Hodge) matrices. Four ways Wakis builds M_ε for increasing geometric fidelity: (1) diagonal Hodge on orthogonal primary/dual pairs, (2) Dey–Mittra conformal cut cell using the open edge length l_k and open face area S_m, (3) tensor subpixel averaging across a tilted dielectric interface with normal n̂, and (4) a symmetric metric tensor on a non-orthogonal curvilinear grid.
figures.visual_intent: A row of four equal square panels, numbered 1 to 4 in small circles, each with a two-to-four word heading. Panel 1 heading 'Orthogonal: diagonal': a 2D square grid cell (blue) with its dual cell (orange, dashed) offset by half a cell; one blue edge of length labelled '|L_k|' crossing an orange dual edge labelled '|Ã_k|' at a right angle with a small right-angle mark; below: '(M_ε)_kk = ε̄_k |Ã_k| / |L_k|'. Panel 2 heading 'Conformal cut cell': a square grid cell cut by a smooth curved grey metal boundary (hatched region labelled 'PEC'); the part of one edge inside vacuum highlighted, labelled 'l_k ≤ |L_k|'; the open part of the cell face shaded, labelled 'S_m ≤ |A_m|'. Panel 3 heading 'Tensor subpixel averaging': a square cell split by a tilted straight line separating two dielectrics, lower region shaded light green labelled 'ε₂', upper region white labelled 'ε₁'; an arrow normal to the interface labelled 'n̂'; three small arrows at different edge positions labelled 'E_x', 'E_y' coupled by a curved double arrow; below: 'symmetric positive definite'. Panel 4 heading 'Curvilinear grid': a patch of a curved, non-orthogonal structured grid (like an O-grid around a circle) with one skewed cell highlighted; its primary face and dual edge meet at a visibly non-right angle; below: '2 × 2 SPD metric'. Across the top of all four panels a thin green banner reading 'approximation lives here: M_ε, M_ν'. Across the bottom a thin grey banner reading 'C and S stay exact on every grid'.

figures.caption: Figure 4.4: Leapfrog time stepping and its stability limit. Left: electric voltages ê live at integer time levels and magnetic fluxes b̂ at half-integer levels; each update uses the most recent other field. Centre: for one eigenmode the amplification factor ξ stays on the unit circle while Δt²λ < 4 (stable, no numerical loss) and leaves it when Δt²λ > 4. Right: below the CFL limit the discrete energy W is constant to round-off; above it the solution grows.
figures.visual_intent: Three panels in a row. LEFT panel: a horizontal time axis labelled 't' with tick labels 'n−1', 'n−½', 'n', 'n+½', 'n+1'. Blue filled circles above integer ticks labelled 'ê' and orange filled squares above half-integer ticks labelled 'b̂'. Curved arrows hop alternately: from ê at n to b̂ at n+½ (arrow label '−Δt C'), then from b̂ at n+½ to ê at n+1 (arrow label 'Δt M_ε⁻¹ Cᵀ M_ν'). Title-free; small caption under axis 'leapfrog: explicit, second order'. CENTRE panel: a complex plane with axes 'Re ξ' and 'Im ξ' and a unit circle. Two blue dots on the circle placed symmetrically above and below the real axis with a small arrow showing them moving along the circle towards −1, labelled 'Δt²λ < 4: |ξ| = 1'. At the point −1 a dot labelled 'Δt²λ = 4'. Two red dots on the real axis, one inside the circle and one outside to the left of −1, labelled 'Δt²λ > 4: |ξ| > 1'. Under the panel the single expression 'Δt < 2 / √λ_max'. RIGHT panel: a schematic plot with horizontal axis 'time step n' and vertical axis 'energy W' (no numbers on axes). A flat blue horizontal line labelled 'below CFL: W constant' and a red curve that starts on the same level then rises steeply labelled 'above CFL: unstable'. Do not put any numeric tick values in any panel.

figures.caption: Figure 4.5: Three derivations, one algebraic system. FDTD reaches the staggered update by Taylor-expanding derivatives on a Cartesian grid; FIT reaches the same equations from integral balances on any primary/dual cell pair; lowest-order edge-element FEM reaches it from a weak form with a lumped mass. On a Cartesian grid FIT with leapfrog is Yee FDTD operation for operation, but the integral view extends to unstructured, cut-cell and subgridded meshes and gives an exact adjoint. Bottom: the discrete exterior calculus dictionary.
figures.visual_intent: Upper two-thirds: three source boxes on the left stacked vertically, each with a tiny pictogram, all with arrows converging to one central box on the right. Box 1 'FDTD: Taylor differences at staggered points' with a pictogram of a small Cartesian Yee cell (cube with E arrows on edges and H arrows on face centres), tag 'Cartesian only'. Box 2 'FIT: integral balances on dual cells' with a pictogram of a triangle mesh with its dual Voronoi polygons dashed, tag 'any cell complex'. Box 3 'FEM: Galerkin weak form + mass lumping' with a pictogram of a tetrahedron with arrows on its edges, tag 'lumped mass → diagonal'. Central target box (dark grey border) containing two lines: 'C ê = −d b̂/dt' and 'Cᵀ ĥ = d d̂/dt + ĵ', with beneath it 'd̂ = M_ε ê,  ĥ = M_ν b̂'. To the right of the central box, three short green check-marked benefits stacked: 'unstructured and cut-cell meshes', 'stable subgridding: keep C̃ = Cᵀ', 'exact discrete adjoint'. Lower third: a horizontal ladder of four grey cells separated by arrows: '0-forms φ (vertices)' → arrow labelled 'G = d₀' → '1-forms E, H (edges)' → arrow labelled 'C = d₁' → '2-forms B, D (faces)' → arrow labelled 'S = d₂' → '3-forms ρ (volumes)'; beneath it 'd_{k+1} d_k = 0' and a green bracket labelled 'Hodge star ⋆ = M_ε, M_ν: primal k ↔ dual (3−k)'.

figures.caption: Figure 4.6: FIT and edge-element FEM share the same Faraday equation and differ only in the mass (Hodge) matrix. Galerkin FEM couples every edge to its neighbours through a sparse non-diagonal mass matrix, so each explicit step needs a linear solve; lumping onto the circumcentric dual gives FIT's diagonal matrix and a solve-free update. The lumped matrix stays positive only when circumcentres lie inside their elements. Right: time-domain FIT gives a broadband spectrum from one run, frequency-domain FEM one solve per frequency.
figures.visual_intent: Three panels. LEFT panel 'Mass matrix': two square sparsity-pattern sketches side by side. The first labelled 'Galerkin FEM M_ε' shows a symmetric scatter of dark blocks around the diagonal (banded, non-diagonal) with caption 'linear solve every step'. The second labelled 'FIT (lumped) M_ε' shows only the main diagonal filled with caption 'no solver: explicit update'. An arrow between them labelled 'mass lumping on the circumcentric dual'. CENTRE panel 'Well-centred mesh?': two small triangle pairs. Top pair: two acute triangles, their circumcentres (orange dots) inside, the dual edge joining the circumcentres crossing the shared edge, labelled 'dual length > 0: stable' with a green check. Bottom pair: one obtuse triangle whose circumcentre lies outside it, the dual edge reversed, labelled 'dual length < 0: indefinite' with a red warning sign, and a small grey note 'remedy: barycentric or Whitney Hodge'. RIGHT panel 'Time vs frequency domain': top half a short pulse waveform in time with an arrow 'FFT' to a broad continuous spectrum curve labelled 'FIT: one run, many frequencies'. Bottom half a row of separate vertical bars at a few discrete frequencies, each bar topped with a small matrix icon, labelled 'FEM: one solve per frequency'. No numeric axis ticks.

figures.caption: Figure 4.7: Where FIT sits among computational electromagnetics methods. Methods are arranged by electrical size of the problem (horizontal) and by what they discretize: the whole volume (FIT, FDTD, FEM, DGTD, FDFD), only surfaces or wires (BEM/MoM), Fourier harmonics in periodic layers (RCWA), or asymptotic rays and wavefronts for very large scenes (ray tracing, Fourier optics).
figures.visual_intent: A wide landscape map. Horizontal axis arrow at the bottom labelled 'electrical size L/λ' with three region labels under it, left to right: 'sub-wavelength', 'a few to hundreds of λ', '≫ 100 λ' (these three phrases are the only axis labels; no numeric ticks). Four horizontal bands stacked vertically, each a light-tinted rounded strip with its band name at the left edge: Band 1 'volume mesh': contains five small cards: 'FIT' (blue, emphasised with a thicker border; pictogram: staggered dual grid), 'FDTD' (pictogram: Cartesian Yee cell), 'FEM' (pictogram: tetrahedra), 'DGTD' (pictogram: triangles with discontinuous colour per element), 'FDFD' (pictogram: grid plus a sparse matrix). Band 2 'surface mesh': card 'BEM / MoM' (pictogram: a triangulated sphere surface and a thin wire). Band 3 'Fourier layers': card 'RCWA' (pictogram: periodic grating layers with plane-wave arrows). Band 4 'asymptotic': cards 'ray tracing' (pictogram: rays reflecting off a lens) and 'Fourier optics' (pictogram: wavefront propagating between two planes). Volume-mesh cards sit at the left/centre of the size axis, BEM/MoM spans centre, RCWA at centre, ray tracing and Fourier optics at the far right. Under each card one short strength phrase in grey: FIT 'exact conservation, broadband, GPU', FDTD 'simple stencil', FEM 'curved high order', DGTD 'high order, local mass', FDFD 'fast 2D direct solve', BEM / MoM 'no volume, exact radiation', RCWA 'periodic stacks', ray tracing 'huge scenes', Fourier optics 'free-space propagation'.

figures.caption: Figure 4.8: What each method has to store and solve. The operator structure explains most of the comparison table: FIT and FDTD apply a sparse curl and a diagonal material matrix with no solve; DGTD inverts small blocks locally; FEM and FDFD factorize a large sparse matrix per frequency; BEM/MoM fills a dense matrix over the surface; RCWA solves a dense eigenproblem per layer; Fourier optics is diagonal in Fourier space.
figures.visual_intent: A row of seven equal tiles, each showing a stylised square matrix sparsity pattern (black/grey cells on white) above a two-line label. Tile 1 'FIT / FDTD': two small matrices side by side, a sparse matrix with a few scattered ±1 entries labelled 'C' and a pure diagonal labelled 'M_ε'; bottom label 'explicit, no solve'. Tile 2 'DGTD': block-diagonal matrix with small equal square blocks on the diagonal; bottom label 'local block inverse'. Tile 3 'FEM (frequency)': sparse banded symmetric matrix with fill-in shown as light grey around the band; bottom label 'sparse factorization per ω'. Tile 4 'FDFD': sparse banded matrix similar to FEM; bottom label 'sparse solve per ω'. Tile 5 'BEM / MoM': completely filled dense matrix; bottom label 'dense, surface only'. Tile 6 'RCWA': a dense square block per layer, three small dense blocks stacked with arrows between them; bottom label 'dense eigenproblem per layer'. Tile 7 'Fourier optics': a diagonal matrix with a small 'FFT' tag on each side; bottom label 'diagonal in k-space'. Under all tiles a thin horizontal arrow from left to right labelled 'more coupling per unknown'. FIT/FDTD tile has a blue border; all others grey. No numbers anywhere.

figures.caption: Figure 4.9: A decision tree for choosing a solver. Start from the question being asked: beams and wakefields, broadband 3D devices, curved 2D scatterers, waveguide modes, single-frequency 2D optimisation, periodic layered structures, thin wires in open space, or very large optical and radio scenes.
figures.visual_intent: A clean left-to-right decision tree. Root node on the left, rounded rectangle: 'What are you solving?'. Eight branches fan out to the right, each branch is a question leaf (white box) followed by an arrow to a recommendation box (blue if it is a Wakis FIT solver, grey otherwise). Branches, top to bottom, exactly: (1) 'beam wakefields and impedance' → blue 'Cartesian FIT + wake solver'; (2) 'broadband 3D devices, S-parameters' → blue 'Cartesian FIT on GPU, or prism FIT for extruded circuits'; (3) 'curved 2D metal or plasmonic scatterers' → two boxes stacked: blue 'triangle FIT + local time stepping (moderate accuracy)' and blue 'high-order DGTD (tight accuracy)'; (4) 'waveguide cross-section modes' → blue 'FIT mode solver' plus grey 'high-order FEM'; (5) '2D, one or two frequencies, optimisation' → grey 'FDFD'; (6) 'periodic layered metasurfaces, gratings' → grey 'RCWA' plus blue 'FIT with Bloch boundaries (sloped 3D walls, broadband)'; (7) 'thin wires in open space' → grey 'MoM / BEM'; (8) 'scenes much larger than 100 λ' → grey 'ray tracing or Fourier optics'. Small legend in a corner: blue box 'FIT solver in Wakis', grey box 'other method'. Use only these phrases; no other text.

figures.caption: Figure 4.10: Six ways FIT can go wrong and the remedy for each: (1) staircased curved boundaries, (2) metal–dielectric cut cells whose averaged permittivity crosses zero, (3) one tiny cell setting the global time step, (4) numerical dispersion behind an ultrarelativistic bunch, (5) negative dual lengths on obtuse triangles, (6) dispersive-material coupling when the plasma frequency times the time step is too large.
figures.visual_intent: A 3 × 2 grid of six equal panels, each with a small red-circled number 1–6, a short red heading for the mechanism at the top and a short green line 'remedy: …' at the bottom. Panel 1 heading 'staircase boundary': a smooth circle (dashed grey) overlaid with a jagged blue staircase approximation on a square grid; remedy 'conformal cut cells or body-fitted mesh'. Panel 2 heading 'ε_eff crosses zero': a single grid cell split by a curved boundary between a metal region labelled 'Re ε < 0' (dark grey) and a dielectric labelled 'ε > 0' (light), one edge crossing both regions highlighted in red with a small resonance spike symbol; remedy 'align edges with the metal: triangles or DGTD'. Panel 3 heading 'smallest cell sets Δt': a coarse grid with one very small cell near a narrow gap highlighted in red, a large clock icon over the coarse region and a tiny clock icon over the small cell; remedy 'local time stepping'. Panel 4 heading 'numerical Cherenkov': a bunch (filled ellipse) moving right along an axis labelled 'β = 1', with grid-scale ripples (red wavy lines) trailing behind it at an angle; remedy 'dispersion-free wake scheme'. Panel 5 heading 'negative dual length': an obtuse triangle with its circumcentre (orange dot) outside the triangle and a red reversed dual edge; remedy 'mesh smoothing or SPD Hodge'. Panel 6 heading 'ADE coupling: ω_p Δt too large': a small timeline with large step marks and a fast oscillation drawn between steps that is under-resolved (red); remedy 'reduce the time step or use a surface impedance'. No numeric values anywhere except those in the headings.
